title: Web Security: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Attack Lab
description: A hands-on cyber range training lab based on the SEED Labs CSRF exercise with Elgg. Students perform GET and POST CSRF attacks, test secret tokens, and analyze SameSite cookies.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of HTTP requests (GET and POST)
Familiarity with HTML forms and JavaScript
Understanding of web browser developer tools
outcomes: Understand the fundamental mechanics of Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).
Forge an HTTP GET request to perform unauthorized state-changing actions.
Forge an HTTP POST request using JavaScript and hidden HTML forms.
Understand and re-enable server-side CSRF secret token verification.
Analyze SameSite cookie attributes (Strict vs Lax vs Normal) and their role in CSRF defense.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# CSRF Attack Lab - Introduction

## Disclaimer
This lab is for **educational purposes only** in an isolated cyber range sandbox.

## Storyline
You are a security researcher assessing the **Elgg** social network platform. The application is vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).

You will act as an attacker (**Samy**) targeting a victim (**Alice**) who has an active session on Elgg.

## Lab Topology & Environment
- **seed** (10.1.30.10): Your workstation running Ubuntu with Firefox and tools.
- **server** (10.1.30.5): Web server hosting Elgg and the attacker site.

### Accessible Sites:
- `http://www.seed-server.com` - Vulnerable Elgg application
- `http://www.attacker32.com` - Attacker malicious website
- `http://www.example32.com` - Defense demonstration site

### Pre-configured Accounts:
- Alice: `alice` / `seedalice`
- Samy: `samy` / `seedsamy`
- Admin: `admin` / `seedelgg`
- Boby: `boby` / `seedboby`

levels.title: Access the Sandbox
levels.cloud_content:
## Connecting to Your Sandbox

1. In the topology view, right-click **seed** and choose **Open GUI**.
2. Login credentials: username **user**, password **Password123**.
3. Open Firefox and verify that `http://www.seed-server.com` loads.
4. When ready, submit **start** to begin the training.

levels.title: Task 1: Observing HTTP Requests
levels.content:
# Task 1: Observing HTTP Requests

Before forging requests, investigate legitimate Elgg requests using Firefox Developer Tools (press F12 -> Network tab).

1. Log in to `http://www.seed-server.com` as **alice** / **seedalice**.
2. In Developer Tools Network tab, watch the request when Alice adds a friend or clicks Add Friend.
3. Note the HTTP method, URL endpoint, and parameters.

Submit the HTTP method used by the Add-Friend action (in UPPERCASE) as the flag.
levels.solution: The Add-Friend request uses the HTTP GET method: http://www.seed-server.com/action/friends/add?friend=...

hints.title: HTTP Method Hint
hints.content: Check the Method column in Firefox Network Developer Tools. Is it GET or POST?

levels.title: Task 2: CSRF Attack via GET Request
levels.content: # Task 2: CSRF Attack via GET Request Samy wants Alice to add him as a friend without her consent. 1. Identify Samy's GUID on Elgg (visit Samy's profile or inspect Add Friend). 2. Edit the attack page `/home/user/Labsetup/attacker/addfriend.html` on your seed machine. 3. Place an `` tag pointing to `http://www.seed-server.com/action/friends/add?friend=`. 4. Log in as Alice in Firefox, then visit `http://www.attacker32.com/addfriend.html` in another tab. 5. Alice will automatically send the GET request and add Samy as a friend! 6. Retrieve your unique flag by running: ```bash curl http://www.seed-server.com:8080/csrf_flag/task2 ```
levels.solution: Embed into addfriend.html. When Alice visits http://www.attacker32.com/addfriend.html, her browser sends the GET request with her session cookie.

hints.title: How to trigger GET automatically?
hints.content: An HTML tag automatically sends a GET request to its src attribute upon page load.

hints.title: Finding Samy GUID
hints.content: Log in as Samy or view Samy profile URL to find his numeric GUID.

levels.title: Task 3: CSRF Attack via POST Request
levels.content:
# Task 3: CSRF Attack via POST Request

Samy wants Alice's profile to say 'Samy is my Hero'.

Profile modification uses an HTTP POST request to `http://www.seed-server.com/action/profile/edit`.

1. Inspect the profile edit POST request parameters in Firefox Developer Tools.
2. Complete `/home/user/Labsetup/attacker/editprofile.html` with JavaScript that constructs and auto-submits a hidden POST form with Alice's GUID and briefdescription='Samy is my Hero'.
3. While logged in as Alice, visit `http://www.attacker32.com/editprofile.html`.
4. Check Alice's profile to verify the change.
5. Retrieve your unique flag by running:
```bash
curl http://www.seed-server.com:8080/csrf_flag/task3
```
levels.solution: Create a hidden form in JavaScript with fields name, briefdescription='Samy is my Hero', accesslevel[briefdescription]=2, and guid=ALICE_GUID, set form.action to http://www.seed-server.com/action/profile/edit, method='post', and call form.submit() on window.onload.

hints.title: Auto-submitting POST form
hints.content: Use document.createElement('form'), append hidden inputs, and call form.submit() inside window.onload.

hints.title: Required Fields
hints.content: Make sure to include name, briefdescription, accesslevel[briefdescription]=2, and guid.

levels.title: Task 4: Enable the CSRF Countermeasure
levels.content:
# Task 4: Enabling Elgg CSRF Secret Token Countermeasure

Elgg has built-in secret token defense (__elgg_token and __elgg_ts). The validation was intentionally disabled in `Csrf.php`.

1. On the server or via docker exec into elgg-10.9.0.5, open:
   `/var/www/elgg/vendor/elgg/elgg/engine/classes/Elgg/Security/Csrf.php`
2. Remove the bypass line: `return; // Added for SEED Labs (disabling the CSRF countermeasure)` from the `validate()` method.
3. Re-test both Task 2 and Task 3 attacks. Notice they now fail because the attacker website cannot guess or steal Alice's secret CSRF token.
4. Retrieve your unique flag by running:
```bash
curl http://www.seed-server.com:8080/csrf_flag/task4
```
levels.solution: Remove the early return statement in validate() inside Csrf.php to re-enable token checking. Forged requests from attacker32.com lack valid tokens and are rejected.

hints.title: Container modification
hints.content: Run docker exec -it elgg-10.9.0.5 /bin/bash to access the container and edit Csrf.php.

hints.title: Why does the attack fail?
hints.content: The Same-Origin Policy prevents attacker32.com from reading the __elgg_token embedded in seed-server.com HTML pages.

levels.title: Task 5: SameSite Cookie Defense
levels.content:
# Task 5: SameSite Cookie Defense

Modern browsers enforce SameSite cookie attributes (Strict, Lax, None) to mitigate CSRF.

1. Visit `http://www.example32.com/` in Firefox. Three cookies are set: cookie-normal, cookie-lax, cookie-strict.
2. Click Link A (same-site navigation) and observe which cookies are sent.
3. Click Link B (cross-site navigation from attacker32.com) and observe which cookies are blocked.
4. Observe that cookie-strict and cookie-lax protect against cross-site requests.
5. Retrieve your unique flag by running:
```bash
curl http://www.seed-server.com:8080/csrf_flag/task5
```
levels.solution: Visiting example32.com sets 3 cookies. In cross-site requests from attacker32.com, SameSite=Strict and SameSite=Lax cookies are not attached to cross-site sub-requests, preventing CSRF.

hints.title: SameSite Cookie types
hints.content: Strict cookies are never sent in cross-site contexts. Lax cookies are only sent with top-level GET navigations.
